item.content:encoded:
Ben Affleck may have an Oscar on his shelf, but his kids clearly don't think he's taking home the trophy for relationship advice.
The 54-year-old actor gave insight into his family dynamics with the three children he shares with ex-wife Jennifer Garner: Violet, 20, Fin, 17, and Samuel, 14. His kids aren't pulling any punches when it comes to Affleck's dating life — they are regularly roasting him.
More from SheKnows
Affleck humorously explained on Jimmy Kimmel Live! how his kids mocked him when he tried to share his "lived experience" while they were talking "about their friends and the drama and their relationships" at the dinner table.
"I said, 'You know, well, the thing about that relationship there with that person…'" Affleck recalled. "The 17-year-old [Fin] just turns to me and goes, 'Oh, like you're the expert on relationships?'"
Oops! Those kids are taking note of the Argo star's divorce from Garner in 2018, and his second marriage to Jennifer Lopez, which also ended in divorce in January 2025.
Affleck realized he had become the "caricature" to his kids — he wasn't the "cool dad" he thought he was going to be.
"I, like, give advice or try to talk to them like a parent, as you do … but what I've found is that now it's not only one teenager rolling their eyes," he added. "I catch them giving each other looks."
And of course, you always have to watch out for the youngest one, who seems to have his dad's number.
"We're just browsing around and there's some book by a French guy, and it's called I'm Sorry for Everything, and my kid immediately turns to me, deadpan, and goes, 'Oh, look, Dad, it's your autobiography,'" he said of son Samuel.
Affleck took the ribbing all in stride, and even mentioned how he was "proud" of his son for his comedic chops.
For Affleck, getting teased by his kids may just be the price for trying to dispense relationship wisdom when your own romantic history gives them plenty of material.

item.title: [Cosmopolitan] Experts Want You to Ignore This TikTok Dating Advice That Could Ruin Your Relationship
item.dc:creator: Syeda Khaula Saad

item.content:encoded:
There is a lot of advice I turn to TikTok for: new exercises for my next glute day, throw pillows that will give my apartment a “fall refresh,” where to buy dupes for expensive makeup. But as a sex and relationships writer, there’s one thing I never take seriously on TikTok: any and all dating advice.
Are there some great, qualified relationship experts giving healthy and meaningful relationship advice on TikTok? Of course! Is a majority of the “relationship advice” on the app total and utter garbage? Also, yes. And because the latter heavily outnumbers the former, whenever I see someone start talking about how “if he wanted to, he would” I immediately scroll away.
There is this weird phenomenon happening on TikTok where people are encouraged to do no work in a relationship and yet expect a partner that is totally perfect. These fake relationship gurus spout “advice” that doesn’t take into account that we’re humans and that relationships take effort and understanding. Also, we’re all told to essentially expect the worst of the each other, have standards that we, ourselves don’t even meet, and of course, treat every relationship like it’s transactional.
“One of the trickiest parts of going to TikTok for dating advice is that short videos don't allow for complexity and nuance,” Elise Braunschweiger, founder and head matchmaker at Amnity Matchmaking tells Cosmopolitan. “Instead, dating advice gets boiled down to its most controversial, click-baity, and scandalous iteration.”
So we asked the real relationship experts (licensed therapists and psychologists) which TikTok advice everyone would be better off leaving alone.
“Test Them.”
TikTok is constantly telling you to test your partner.
“This can involve things like purposely ignoring your partner, taking a long time to reply to their messages, acting distant, or creating a situation just to see how they react,” therapist Ronald Hoang explains.
While you may think you’re simply trying to figure out how much your partner cares, you’re basically creating more problems in your relationship.
“Instead of encouraging honest communication, it encourages people to play games and expect their partner to figure out what they are thinking,” Hoang says.
Plus, these tests don’t necessarily prove anything. People have different reactions to things, and just because a reaction doesn’t fit perfectly into what you were expecting doesn’t mean your partner doesn’t care for you.
“A healthier approach would be to communicate directly about what you need from your partner rather than deliberately putting them in a situation where they can fail a test they didn’t know they were taking,” Hoang says.
“They Should Automatically Know What You Want.”
Anytime I hear “if he wanted to, he would” my eyes roll so far back into my head I’m afraid they won’t ever come back out again. The problem with this advice is that it encourages people to stop communicating their needs with their partners. Instead, they immediately cast partners off as “inconsiderate” if they don’t meet your needs.
“We've started confusing emotional compatibility with emotional mind-reading,” Rebecca Boone, clinical director says. “Your partner can love you deeply and still misunderstand you, need something different from you, or get it wrong sometimes.”
Instead of punishing our partners for not reading our minds, we should be open to telling them exactly what it is we want and need out of a relationship. If you just keep your mouth shut and wait to see what your partner does, you’re setting your relationship up for failure.
“Any Relationship Friction Is a Red Flag.”
I’ve heard people on TikTok say that “relationships shouldn’t be hard.” And while sure, every day with your partner shouldn’t feel like exhausting physical labor, sometimes being with someone can be difficult—that doesn’t automatically mean you should throw the relationship away.
And yet, TikTok relationship “experts” claim that any little issue is a larger symptom of a bad relationship.
“Not every disagreement is gaslighting, not every need for space is avoidant attachment, and not every uncomfortable interaction means you're in a toxic relationship,” Boone says. “These terms describe real patterns, but when we use them to explain every difficult moment, we can lose the ability to distinguish between a relationship that needs repair and one that is genuinely harmful.”
The reality is that even healthy relationships activate our insecurities sometimes. But it’s about how you navigate communication, accountability, and emotional safety afterward.
“The question shouldn't always be, ‘Did my partner trigger me?’” Boone says. “Sometimes the more useful question is, ‘What happened after I was triggered? Were we able to talk about it, take responsibility, and find our way back to each other?’”
“Be Alert at All Times.”
TikTok relationship advice pushes you to constantly assess and overanalyze your relationship to look for red flags.
“Being overly tuned in to relationship content can create hypervigilance in your relationship,” psychotherapist Ciara Bogdanovic, LMFT says. It can mean that you’re constantly worried about what you deserve, ending up with a “loser,” what you need to fix, and what’s wrong in your relationship.
“It impedes your ability to truly be present in your relationship and enjoy your partner’s company, and instead creates anxiety about whether your relationship is good enough,” Bogdanovic says. “The issues manifest internally as anxiety and externally as arguments and tension with your partner.”
Sure, you should be aware of any concerning behaviors. But if you’re constantly looking for red flags, you’re going to create some on your own. It’s okay to be comfortable in your relationship. In fact, that should be your goal.
“Relationships Are for Financial Gain, Not Romantic Connection.”
I’ll admit, I thought the “sprinkle sprinkle” content was funny—until I realized people were taking it seriously.
Now, people look for different things in relationships. And if you truly are only interested in a partnership for financial support, more power to you (I know how expensive groceries are). But TikTok sometimes pushes the idea that all women should look to men to be providers—and it feels pretty “tradwife” or “manosphere” coded if I’m being honest.
AASECT certified sex & couples therapist Vanessa Cushing says that she understands where this idea comes from: Women often are expected to carry a majority of the emotional labor, household chores, and responsibility of raising children. As a response, people on TikTok have encouraged women to seek out men who at least have money to bring to the table.
“When we get into seeking partners based on what they can provide it creates a dynamic where the relationship becomes transactional,” Cushing says. “Relationships should be about the connection—you know you love someone when you just want to hangout with them. You love their essence—how kind they are how loving they are—not how much they can provide for you.”
While we’d all love to be taken care of, this can be done in more ways than just financially.
“If They’re Not Interested In Sex, Go Cold.”
Apparently there are plenty of people telling men on TikTok that if their partner isn’t interested in sex, they should “let her feel the loss.”
I’m sorry—huh?
I get it, being rejected sucks—which is the feeling these people are monetizing off of.
“A man who’s been rejected over and over finally hears something that makes him feel in control again,” Stephanie Flood, LMFT, says. “Yet, for most women, physical connection follows emotional connection.”
This truly is a manosphere talking point. So let’s get to what you should really do: If you’re noticing that your partner hasn’t been as interested in sex, instead of jumping into defense mode, try understanding what’s happening. Have a conversation. Be open-minded. It could be that your partner isn’t feeling great, they’re super stressed, or you’re just not fostering the emotional connection needed for them to want to be physical with you. “Going cold” will do nothing more than get you closer to a breakup.

item.content:encoded:
Column by Penny Newton-Hurley
DUA Lipa recently shared her wedding advice: experience the day as a guest would and stay close to your husband.
Both concern being present and connected each day.
That matters beyond the wedding.
Long-term relationships can falter when practical conversations replace emotional ones.
We talk about school runs, shopping, bills and appointments, but stop asking: “How are you, really?”
When a partner says, “You’re never here,” the words may sound accusing.
Underneath them might be loneliness and a longing for closeness.
The listener hears criticism and replies defensively: “I’m working to support us.”
Now both people are protecting themselves and neither feels understood.
Try slowing the exchange down.
Separate the fact from the judgement, identify the feeling and consider what is needed.
“I’ve noticed we haven’t spent an evening together this week. I miss you and would love time to reconnect. Could we keep Friday evening free?”
This does not guarantee the answer will be yes.
But it makes connection more likely than blame does.
This approach is part of the four-stage MECAnism in my book, The Human Language, out now.
It helps us recognise our thoughts, emotions and core needs before deciding what to say or do.
Staying close on a wedding day is lovely advice.
Staying curious, emotionally honest and connected throughout the days that follow is what sustains a relationship.
The photographs may capture the celebration, but it is the quieter conversations afterwards that build a marriage.
Penny Newton-Hurley is an Oakridge-based communication consultant and mediator.
Her new book, The Human Language, is out now, priced £12.99, and available from bookshops and Amazon.

item.content:encoded:
HBO and Sky Television's upcoming legal drama, War, starring Dominic West and Sienna Miller, will be released on October 1 and 2, respectively. Created by George Kay, this legal series will follow the lives of London's most powerful lawyers from firms Taylor & Byrne and Cathcarts & Sons as they clash over a pivotal legal battle. Season 1 will follow the divorce of British tech entrepreneur Morgan Henderson (Dominic West) and film star Carla Duval (Sienna Miller) as the legal firms race to secure victory for their respective clients.
At the London premiere of their upcoming legal drama, Sienna Miller and Dominic West weighed in on divorce. Speaking to the Associated Press on whether people would think of getting a divorce after watching War, Miller said,
"They might rethink a divorce."
West added that the series does not recommend couples getting a divorce. He advised couples to resolve differences outside the court. While the reporter asked whether living in different countries would help, West said that it was a great idea.
Here's more about it.
War London premiere: Sienna Miller says prenups defeat the purpose of marriage
At the London premiere, Miller said that prenups defeat the purpose of a marriage. She told the Press Association (via The Standard):
"I feel like it kind of defeats the purpose of going into a marriage and making that commitment. But I also understand."
The series is set to explore how prenups are usually not legally binding or enforceable by courts in Wales and England. West called it a waste of time. West added that he loves legal dramas and, most importantly, the twists and turns they contain.
Advertisement
War: Release date, cast, and more about the upcoming HBO legal drama
War was initially announced in 2025 when HBO teamed up with Sky for two seasons. Currently, Season 2 is in production, and Marisa Tomei, David Harewood, and Kelly Macdonald will guest star in Season 2.
War Season 1 will premiere on Thursday, October 1, 2026, at 9 PM ET on HBO. Apart from Miller and West, Season 1 stars Phoebe Fox as Serena Byrne, James McArdle as Nicholas Taylor, Nina Sosanya as "Her Majesty" Beatrice "Queen Bea" Ubosi, and Pip Torrens as John Smallwood. It also features Archie Renaux as Jonathan "Johnny" Warren.
Season 1 will also be available in Italy, Ireland, Germany, Switzerland, Australia, Austria, France, Asia, and Belgium. NBCUniversal Global TV Distribution is responsible for the global sales. It is produced by New Pictures, a Banijay Company, and Observatory Pictures, in association with Sky and HBO.
Speaking to Variety, Kay, who also serves as the writer and executive producer of the series, said that he was eager to go to a mainstream TV show. He added that he had previously worked on thrillers and crime shows, but now he is eager to do character-driven, high-end shows.
"I was thinking about doing this legal show because I love the idea that a case that you’re working on as a lawyer is a kind of metaphor for your own life, where you’re constantly bringing the personal into the professional."
Speaking about War, he added that it is about two high-end rival London law firms. He explained he wanted to do one traditional and older firm and another fresh, ambitious firm with fewer resources but full of smart characters.
"No one’s dusty, but there’s the traditional one, and there’s the modern one. Each season we can come back and reboot with guest star clients."

item.content:encoded:
This article has been reviewed by a Digital Journal editor and may be licensed for reuse.
Artificial intelligence is moving into parts of life that once depended almost entirely on human conversation. A 2026 Marriage.com survey of 1,000 married U.S. adults found that 44% had used an AI tool for relationship advice. Separately, a September 2026 Elon University survey found that 27% of internet-using U.S. adults use AI for personal, emotional, or social interactions, a category that included relationship advice and romantic conversations.
Those figures do not necessarily suggest that chatbots are replacing counselors or partners. They may simply show that some people are turning to AI to think through conflict, uncertainty, or difficult emotions. Its accessibility may be part of the appeal, although relationship issues can involve perspectives and context that AI cannot fully capture.
Relationship questions can be particularly difficult for automated systems because the information they receive is usually limited to what one person chooses to provide. A response may therefore reflect only part of a disagreement, without access to the other person’s intentions, experiences, or interpretation of the same situation.
That limitation may matter when people use AI to interpret a partner’s words or decide how to respond to conflict. General guidance can offer another perspective, but relationship decisions often depend on context, communication, and an understanding of both people involved.
Sheila J. Simpson, executive director of FOCCUS Marriage Ministries, believes that convenience deserves to be separated from judgment. Her concern is not that couples use technology, but that they may give it a role that belongs more appropriately to direct conversation or qualified human support. “AI can offer immediate access when someone wants to think through a question,” she explains. “But I believe that convenience should complement, rather than replace, the perspective and understanding that can come from human relationships.”
The organization’s FOCCUS Pre-Marriage Inventory can be completed online, with the results used to generate reports that support subsequent discussion between the couple and a trained facilitator. The process then returns to guided human conversation. Simpson sees that sequence as important because a report can organize information, while a person can help two partners explore what those responses mean in the context of their own relationship.
“We only take technology to a point, and then we recognize that there has to be human intervention and discussion,” Simpson says. “Every relationship is unique. So, every solution must fit those unique circumstances.”
That becomes especially relevant when one partner asks an AI system to interpret an argument. The prompt usually reflects one person’s memory, wording, assumptions, and emotional state. The other partner is not present to clarify what they intended or how they experienced the same moment.
Simpson believes that limitations can be easy to overlook when an AI system feels highly personalized. “AI can’t read minds,” she notes. “You’re asking AI the question based on your assumptions to begin with, because that other person is not part of that discussion.”
Recent research gives that concern additional context. A 2026 study examining 11 AI models found that sycophantic responses, meaning responses that excessively affirm a user, could increase users’ confidence that they were right while reducing their willingness to repair interpersonal conflict. Simpson notes that the findings do not mean every chatbot response will reinforce one side, but they illustrate why agreement can be a weak substitute for understanding.
This also brings psychological safety into the conversation. Both people need enough space to express themselves honestly, clarify what they mean, and feel that their perspective has been heard. “Relationships are shaped by different histories, cultures, goals, habits, and expectations,” she explains. “Advice can offer a useful starting point, but it still has to be considered in the context of the two people involved.”
That does not leave AI without a constructive role. Simpson sees value in using it to identify resources, terminology, or types of professional support that someone may not know exist. “AI may be most useful when it helps someone identify the right professional resource,” she explains. “Rather than replacing expert guidance, it can help direct people toward qualified professionals who are better placed to support them.”
That distinction may become more important as AI becomes easier to consult. A chatbot can help someone organize a question or identify possible sources of support, but Simpson believes it should not take the place of direct communication between partners. “AI may help someone think through what they want to ask,” she explains. “But when the issue involves the relationship itself, I believe the next step should be to bring that conversation back to the two people involved.”
AI may help people organize their thoughts or find support, but Simpson believes the most important conversations should remain between the people in the relationship. As these tools become easier to use, the goal should be to support communication, not replace it.
